title: AI Snake Oil
subtitle: What Artificial Intelligence Can Do, What It Can't, and How to Tell the Difference
pitch: Two Princeton computer scientists separate real AI progress from hype, and argue advanced AI is not an existential threat. The best skeptical counterweight on this shelf.

chapters.g: Why 'AI' covers very different technologies, and what snake oil means here: AI that does not and cannot work as advertised.
Systems that predict who will commit crimes, fail at school or get sick often fail, and can entrench inequality.

chapters.t: Why Can't AI Predict the Future?
chapters.g: The Fragile Families Challenge and other evidence that predicting life outcomes is hard for any method.

chapters.t: The Long Road to Generative AI
chapters.g: A clear history of generative AI, what it is good at and its real harms.

chapters.t: Is Advanced AI an Existential Threat?
chapters.g: The authors' case against existential risk worries: they expect gradual change and think defences should focus on misuse.

chapters.t: Why Can't AI Fix Social Media?
chapters.g: Content moderation is about values and context, which AI cannot settle on its own.

chapters.t: Why Do Myths about AI Persist?
chapters.g: How companies, researchers and journalists keep hype alive.

chapters.t: Where Do We Go from Here?
chapters.g: Practical advice for readers, policymakers and companies.

ideas: Generative AI and predictive AI are very different, and predictive AI often fails.
Much AI hype comes from incentives, not evidence.
The authors do not see advanced AI as an existential threat.
Focus on what people do with AI.

args.a: Fears of rogue superintelligence are overblown.
args.c: Safety researchers point to recent evidence like scheming, alignment faking and shutdown resistance as reasons to take rogue AI seriously.

args.a: We should worry about what people do with AI more than what AI does on its own.
args.c: Many think both matter and that misuse and misalignment risks grow together.

questions: Read this next to If Anyone Builds It. Which arguments moved you, and why?
Where have you seen AI snake oil in India, for example in hiring or education?

quiz.q: What do the authors mean by 'AI snake oil'?
o: AI that does not and cannot work as advertised
quiz.w: It is AI sold with claims it cannot meet.

quiz.q: Which kind of AI do they criticise most?
quiz.w: Predictive AI for life outcomes often fails.

quiz.q: What is their view on existential risk from AI?
o: It is not a serious threat on their analysis
quiz.w: Chapter 5 argues against treating advanced AI as an existential threat.
